analyses.title: Implicit Argument Prediction with Event Knowledge
analyses.research_question: Can distributed event knowledge and entity-salience information improve prediction of implicit arguments whose fillers occur elsewhere in a document?
analyses.methodology: The paper introduces an argument-cloze formulation in which one argument of an event is removed and the model must select its filler from entities mentioned elsewhere in the document. Event representations are learned from a large English Wikipedia corpus, and a neural coherence model scores candidate entities using event compatibility together with salience features. The model is evaluated on two OntoNotes-derived cloze settings and is additionally adapted to the natural implicit-argument dataset of Gerber and Chai.

key_findings.finding: Combining learned event knowledge with entity-salience features substantially improves argument-cloze accuracy over frequency and simpler event-embedding baselines.
On the shorter OntoNotes setting, the 40-million-example EventComp model with salience reaches 47.75% accuracy, compared with 41.89% without salience and 22.76% for the most-frequent-entity baseline.
On the longer and more entity-dense OntoNotes setting, the 40-million-example EventComp model with salience reaches 27.87% accuracy, outperforming the corresponding model without salience at 21.79%.

For the Gerber-Chai natural implicit-argument task, successive adaptations for deciding whether a role is filled, handling multiple roles, and adding salience raise the 40-million-example EventComp system to 49.6 F1.
key_findings.section: Evaluation on naturally occurring implicit arguments / Table 6

key_findings.finding: The final adapted system approaches the original Gerber-Chai result while exceeding the authors' automatically reproducible Gerber-Chai baseline, suggesting that broad event knowledge can substitute for some manually engineered resources.
key_findings.section: Evaluation on naturally occurring implicit arguments and Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Among the tested salience signals, mention-count information contributes most of the gain, while first-mention location and head-count features provide little or negative additional benefit in the reported ablation.

limitations: The argument-cloze benchmark is synthetically constructed by deleting otherwise explicit event arguments, so it is only a proxy for naturally omitted arguments.
The natural implicit-argument evaluation is small and restricted to ten nominal predicates, limiting conclusions about broader predicate and discourse coverage.
The experiments concern Wikipedia and newswire-style text rather than authentic workplace email or enterprise chat.
The formulation predicts entity fillers for event roles; it does not annotate workplace-specific assignees, group assignees, decisions, deadlines, or action-to-deadline links.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not represented as target structures.
Candidate fillers are entities/coreference chains rather than arbitrary exact evidence spans, so the task does not directly evaluate exact argument-span extraction.
The natural-task adaptation relies on mapping nominal predicates and semantic roles into the model's verbal/syntactic event representation.
The paper releases code but does not state that its generated cloze instances are distributed as a standalone benchmark dataset.
raw_claims: Implicit arguments are arguments that are not syntactically attached to their predicates but may have fillers elsewhere in the surrounding discourse.
The proposed argument-cloze task removes one event argument and asks a model to recover its entity from the other entities in the document.
The training resources are automatically derived from a large English Wikipedia dump using dependency parsing and coreference information.
The EventComp architecture scores narrative coherence between the event with the missing role and events associated with candidate entities.
Entity salience is represented with features including mention frequency, first-mention location, and head-mention count.
The OntoNotes evaluation uses gold dependency and coreference information to construct controlled argument-cloze cases.
The longer-document test set is harder because each document contains substantially more candidate entities.
Adding salience improves both short- and long-document cloze performance for the EventComp models.
The model must be modified to handle whether an implicit role should be filled and to predict several roles for the Gerber-Chai task.
The best adapted model achieves 49.6 F1 on the Gerber-Chai evaluation.
The authors identify richer global narrative-coherence modeling as a direction for future work.

analyses.title: Multi-Sentence Argument Linking
analyses.research_question: Can a document-level model reliably link event roles to argument spans across sentence boundaries, and can a new large-scale benchmark support progress on this task?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct RAMS, a corpus of 9,124 annotated event instances covering 139 event types, from English news documents, with annotators selecting argument spans in a five-sentence window around each event trigger. They formulate multi-sentence argument linking as scoring combinations of an event, a semantic role, and a candidate span, using contextual representations and an explicit null candidate for unattested roles. Experiments compare several baselines and model variants on RAMS, examine sentence-distance effects and decoding constraints, and test transfer to AIDA, BNB, and GVDB datasets.

key_findings.finding: RAMS contains 9,124 annotated event instances from 3,993 news documents, with 139 event types, 65 role types, and 21,237 annotated argument links.

Although most RAMS arguments occur in the trigger sentence, arguments in neighboring sentences remain common enough to motivate document-level linking, with 82% of annotated arguments reported as sentence-local.
With gold trigger and gold argument spans supplied, the main model obtains 68.3 test F1, and type-constrained decoding using gold event types raises test F1 to 73.3.

When the system must consider all possible spans instead of being given gold argument spans, performance drops to about 6 F1, showing that candidate-span identification is a major unresolved end-to-end difficulty.
Performance on arguments one or two sentences from the trigger is comparable to performance on local arguments in the reported development-set analysis.
Pretraining on RAMS improves downstream AIDA argument-linking performance relative to training only on the smaller AIDA data.
Exact annotation boundaries are materially less consistent than coarse agreement about whether a role is present: pairwise exact span-boundary agreement is reported as 55.3%.

limitations: RAMS is derived from news articles rather than workplace email or enterprise chat, so its discourse structure and participant roles differ from the target domain.
The ontology describes event-semantic roles rather than workplace actions, decisions, assignees, deadlines, or action-to-deadline relations.
Implicit or group assignees are not annotated as dedicated phenomena.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are outside the annotation scheme.
The main high-scoring experiments assume gold argument spans and gold trigger spans, substantially simplifying exact evidence-span extraction.
End-to-end performance when all spans are candidates is very low relative to the gold-span setting.
Annotators are restricted to a five-sentence window and are instructed to choose the closest argument span for a role, which can exclude other valid discourse mentions.
Exact span-boundary agreement is only 55.3%, indicating substantial ambiguity for evaluations that demand exact argument evidence.
The five-sentence context design is based on event extraction in news and may not transfer to long email threads or enterprise-chat conversations.
raw_claims: RAMS is designed to study linking an event's semantic roles to argument spans that may occur outside the trigger sentence.
Each annotation example presents a five-sentence context centered on a typed event trigger.
Argument annotations are represented by token-level start and end offsets.
Annotators select the closest available span for each role when more than one mention could fill it.
The completed RAMS corpus contains 9,124 event instances and more than twenty-one thousand argument annotations.
Eighty-two percent of the annotated arguments are in the same sentence as their event trigger.
The model represents a potential link using the event, role, candidate span, and their contextual interactions.
A null argument option is used for roles that are not explicitly instantiated in the context.
The strongest main RAMS result relies on gold candidate argument spans and type-constrained decoding.
Removing the gold-span assumption causes a large performance decline.
Agreement on exact argument boundaries is markedly lower than agreement on whether an argument exists.
RAMS pretraining provides useful transfer to the smaller AIDA event-argument dataset.
The paper makes its RAMS data and implementation available through the project site.

analyses.title: Semantic Role Labeling of Implicit Arguments for Nominal Predicates
analyses.research_question: Can implicit semantic arguments of nominal predicates be identified and linked to discourse constituents using supervised features derived from lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse resources?
analyses.methodology: The authors manually annotate implicit arguments for ten frequent NomBank nominal predicates in Penn Treebank Wall Street Journal documents, producing annotations for 1,247 predicate instances. Candidate fillers are drawn primarily from gold PropBank and NomBank arguments within a two-sentence preceding window, and a LibLinear classifier ranks candidates using a large collection of lexical, semantic, syntactic, distance, and discourse features. Performance is evaluated with randomized ten-fold cross-validation using overlap-based precision, recall, and F1, and is compared with a nearest-candidate baseline, an oracle, and a limited human annotation study.

key_findings.finding: Adding manually identified implicit arguments increases semantic-role coverage for the ten studied nominal predicates by roughly 20 absolute percentage points, corresponding to a reported 71% relative increase over NomBank's explicit-role coverage.
The discriminative system achieves 57.9 precision, 44.5 recall, and 50.3 F1 on filled implicit arguments, compared with 28.9 F1 for the baseline.
The oracle reaches 87.6 F1, indicating that a substantial portion of remaining error comes from candidate generation and search-window restrictions rather than only candidate ranking.
Approximately 31% of analyzed system errors arise because the true filler is either absent from the candidate set despite being in the window or lies outside the two-sentence window.
Semantic-role compatibility is among the strongest predictive feature classes, while sentence distance also contributes strongly to filler selection.
The paper's manually created implicit-argument annotations are stated to be freely available for research use.

limitations: The annotated corpus covers only ten nominal predicates, and several model features are lexicalized to those predicates, limiting generalization to unseen predicates.
The source documents are Wall Street Journal newswire rather than workplace email or enterprise chat.
The task models semantic arguments of nominal predicates, not explicit workplace action items, decisions, assignees, group assignees, deadlines, or action-to-deadline bindings.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not target annotations.
Evaluation uses a Dice-style span-overlap measure rather than strict exact-span matching, making the reported scores unsuitable as direct evidence for exact argument-evidence extraction.
The system uses gold PropBank and NomBank annotations for candidate generation and feature computation, which is a strong assumption for deployment on raw text.
Candidate search is mainly restricted to two sentences before the nominal predicate and has an estimated recall ceiling below complete discourse coverage.
Predicate instances are randomized for ten-fold cross-validation rather than split by document, so instances from the same document can potentially occur in different folds.
Annotation disagreement is concentrated in deciding whether an implicit filler exists, showing that even the existence of some roles can be ambiguous.
Joint interactions among several implicit roles are handled only indirectly rather than by a globally structured prediction model.
raw_claims: The study extends semantic role labeling to arguments of nominal predicates that are not locally expressed in the nominal's syntactic structure.
The manually annotated corpus is based on Wall Street Journal sections of the Penn Treebank and focuses on ten NomBank nominal predicates.
The corpus contains 1,247 studied predicate instances and hundreds of implicit argument fillers.
Annotators search surrounding discourse for constituents that fill semantic roles missing from the original NomBank annotation.
Most system candidates are existing gold PropBank or NomBank argument constituents.
The classifier uses lexical, syntactic, semantic, salience, distance, and discourse-related features to rank candidate fillers.
The candidate search window is limited primarily to the two sentences preceding a target predicate.
The discriminative model reaches 50.3 F1 and clearly outperforms the nearest-candidate baseline.
The oracle score is much higher than the learned system's score, leaving substantial room for better candidate generation and ranking.
A sizeable fraction of errors occurs because the correct argument is outside the candidate set or outside the search window.
The authors note that lexicalized feature design and the limited predicate inventory constrain generalization.
The manually created annotations are made available for research use.

analyses.title: Reading between the Lines: Information Extraction from Industry Requirements
analyses.research_question: Can scope, applicability conditions, and demanded behavior be extracted from authentic industrial requirement sentences when some of that information is implicit in document context?
analyses.methodology: The authors extract requirement sentences from 23 English DNV rule documents and annotate three semantic components: scope, condition, and demand. Requirements are identified through the modal verb "shall," and two dataset variants are created, one containing only the sentence and another enriched with hierarchical document context and related noun chunks. RoBERTa token-classification models are evaluated with five-fold cross-validation, while GPT-3 text-davinci-003 is tested in a similarity-selected few-shot setup; both are also evaluated on 400 sentences from four held-out documents using ROUGE-L, BLEU-1, and embedding similarity.

key_findings.finding: The final annotated training collection contains 2,147 requirement sentences from 23 authentic DNV industry documents, and contextual annotation yields substantially more scope spans than sentence-only annotation because scope is frequently implicit outside the requirement sentence.

Adding document context produces the largest improvement for scope extraction with RoBERTa, whose average scope scores on the held-out test rise from 0.45 to 0.70 ROUGE-L, 0.43 to 0.62 BLEU-1, and 0.55 to 0.77 embedding similarity.
Condition and demand extraction change comparatively little when context is added to the RoBERTa input, consistent with these components being more often explicit in the requirement sentence itself.
Without contextual input, GPT-3 performs better than RoBERTa on the reported scope and demand text-similarity measures, whereas contextual RoBERTa becomes stronger on scope.

The authors' contextual representation does not produce a comparable scope gain for the GPT-3 few-shot system, suggesting that its prompting setup does not exploit the supplied context as effectively as the supervised sequence-labeling model.

The requirement representation explicitly separates applicability condition from demanded behavior, making condition extraction a first-class span-labeling problem rather than folding it into the demand text.

limitations: The source is authentic industry documentation but not workplace email or enterprise chat, so it does not model conversational participants, thread structure, or assignments.

Requirements are selected by the presence of the word "shall"; the study therefore does not establish coverage for requirements expressed through other modal, permissive, prohibitive, conditional, or indirect constructions.
The schema contains scope, condition, and demand but no assignee or group-assignee field.
There is no explicit deadline representation or relation linking a demanded action to a deadline.
Although condition spans are annotated, the task does not model logical scope of negation or modal operators over particular actions or arguments.
The reported evaluation metrics are ROUGE-L, BLEU-1, and embedding similarity rather than strict exact-span precision, recall, or F1, so exact evidence-boundary quality is not directly established.
Gold annotations were created primarily by the first author and only a subset was independently validated; no full inter-annotator agreement statistic is reported.
The context representation uses document headings and related noun chunks, which differs substantially from email-thread and chat-conversation context.
The GPT-3 baseline depends on the proprietary text-davinci-003 service, reducing exact reproducibility.
The paper does not report a public release of the annotated dataset or implementation.
raw_claims: The paper treats an industry requirement as containing a scope, an applicability condition, and a demanded behavior.
The intended logical interpretation is that entities within the scope that satisfy the condition must satisfy the demand.
The authors obtain requirements from 23 English DNV rule documents that reflect real industrial classification and risk-management practice.
Sentences containing "shall" are used to identify requirement candidates in these documents.
After annotation filtering, the dataset contains 2,147 requirement sentences.
The contextual version supplies document hierarchy information and noun chunks associated with the same requirement number.
Scope is frequently recoverable only from context rather than from the isolated requirement sentence.
RoBERTa is trained as a token-level sequence-labeling model for scope, condition, and demand.
The GPT-3 experiment uses ten demonstrations chosen according to semantic similarity and requests structured scope, condition, and demand output.
Four additional documents provide a 400-sentence held-out evaluation set spanning both similar and different subject areas.
Context substantially improves supervised scope extraction but has much smaller effects on condition and demand extraction.
The study evaluates generated or extracted component text with ROUGE-L, BLEU-1, and sentence-embedding similarity rather than strict exact-boundary scoring.
